Geometric Image Reconstruction

An FPGA-accelerated geometric image reconstruction tool that recreates input images using semi-transparent polygons and hill-climbing optimization.

Team Anjelica Bian, Mark Franklin, Mac Marsh

Platform DE1-SoC

Core idea Generate, score, mutate, and draw polygons until the target image emerges.

Project Introduction High Level Design Program/Hardware Design Geometric Image Reconstruction Examples Results Conclusions Appendices References

Project Introduction

For our final project we have created a novel FPGA-accelerated geometric image reconstruction tool that can take any input image and recreate it with any number of semi-transparent polygons.

At a high level, our project was built to explore the idea that "Mathematics and art are just two different languages that can be used to express the same ideas” (Richard Feynman). We hope that our analytical, geometric recreation of famous artworks and photos will inspire thoughts as to how we perceive the world, how our brain takes shortcuts to decode information from our eyes, how artists create, and how a finite set of simple things (properly positioned) can form something incredibly complex. In short, we are attempting to make visible one possible translation between mathematics and art.

The user controls the inputs (eg: number of polygons, target artwork, transparency, color mode, etc) and can save the output as a .bmp to their local computer. We built this program to explore the nature of art and its mathematical reconstruction. Furthermore, we were extremely interested in pseudo-random, distributed algorithms resulting in our produced solution. Our final project can produce anything from abstract art to near-realism. Since our algorithm utilizes random seeding, no two outputs are the same - it produces one of a kind artwork every single time!

Project Rationale

Our project idea builds off existing programs that reproduce artwork geometric shapes through the same variant of simulated annealing or hill climbing, specifically [1], [2], and [3]. In December of 2008, Roger Johansson, a Swedish programmer, posted a blog titled “Genetic Programming: Evolution of Mona Lisa.” In this blog post, he described a “small program that keeps a string of DNA for polygon rendering” that could reproduce the Mona Lisa with 50 semi-transparent polygons [1]. The beauty of this program was that it could replicate the Mona Lisa with such a small number of polygons. The way it did this was by mutating the polygon-DNA and grading the result against the whole canvas, keeping improved mutations. This implementation spurred us to wonder if we could do something similar but fully decentralized, i.e. every polygon would only know about itself and the target pixels underneath it. In doing so, we could write an algorithm that would be fully parallelizable for an FPGA. About ten years ago, Michael Fogleman, a software engineer at Formlabs, was inspired by Johansson, and wrote his own version. His algorithm made use of simple hill climbing (accept improved mutations) and he wrote it in Go for fastest possible performance. He highlighted “Partial image difference for faster scoring (only pixels that change need be considered)” as an accelerant which was part of our inspiration for further improvements. Fogleman in turn motivated Sam Twidale to create Geometrize, which features a well-developed user interface that allows anyone to enter their own images and customize their output. This got us thinking about the functionality that we wanted to add for our users!

As a whole we tried to pull together the different strengths of these prior implementations with a completely novel spin - we could not find evidence of anyone attempting this challenge on an FPGA nor through a fully decentralized algorithm.

High Level Design

The project combines prior geometric-art ideas with a decentralized scoring approach designed for FPGA acceleration.

Project Overview

Building on these sources, our project created artistic approximations of reference images by iteratively drawing colored polygons onto a VGA display. The system started with a target image (e.g., Mona Lisa), generated random candidate polygons, evaluated how well each polygon matched the corresponding region of the target image, and used hill climbing to keep polygon mutations that improved the approximation, as measured by a modified sum-of-squared-errors objective function.

From a top level, the project can be grouped into three stages: image preparation, polygon optimization and hill-climbing, and VGA drawing/image display. First, a reference image was converted into binary color data (either 8-bit RGB numbers or 16-bit RGB numbers), rescaled, and loaded into memory in an ARM-side global C array. Then, the program generated numerous random mutations of polygons and used a sum-of-squared errors objective function to measure how well each one matched the underlying target image. Those that best-matched the target image best were drawn to the VGA-display, gradually building out the final discretized polygonal approximation.

As shown in Figure 2, the top level algorithm consisted of a continuous loop: create a polygon, mutate it, check score, choose the best approximation, and repeat. We found 100 iterations to be a sweet spot between quality of output and computation time - in other words, each polygon had 100 mutations to reach its lowest possible score. This gave each polygon ample opportunity to “climb” to a local minimum without making the program unnecessarily slow. The entire output thus consisted of numerous polygons which had all been optimized through a simple hill-climbing algorithm.

We also experimented with a non-constant number of iterations to see if we could improve the result. First, we tried an “early exit” wherein the algorithm would stop early if the polygon had reached some score threshold that indicated a good fit. We found it difficult to quantify this threshold as a “good score” for a large polygon trying to match the background is very different from a good score for a small polygon trying to fit Mona Lisa’s eye. Similarly, we ran into a similar issue when trying to enforce a minimum score for a polygon to be plotted - it was difficult to find a minimum that enforced quality on background shapes without cutting out all of the detailed polygons. We also experimented with different types of mutations: notably a shift of the entire shape. We had hoped this would break our algorithm out of local minimums and improve the quality of the finished product. Unfortunately, as we were experimenting with this, we found that the aforementioned difficult “detail shapes” (eg: a facial feature, or part of the hand) would shift out of the high-difficulty regions to produce an improved score. As previously mentioned, the design of our novel algorithm was the result of our own algorithmic “hill-climbing.”The merits of each change were evaluated by our printout of the average SSE (sum of squared errors) achieved as well as our own visual analysis of the finished product.

Background Math

To evaluate each candidate polygon, the continuous geometric object must first be converted into a discrete set of image pixels. Let a polygon P be defined by vertices:

(x1, y1), (x2, y2), …, (xn, yn)

Rasterization determines the set of pixels belonging to the polygon:

R(P) = { (x, y) ∈ ℤ2 : (x, y) lies inside P }

where ℤ2 represents the discrete pixel grid of the image. In our implementation, rasterization was performed using a scanline algorithm, limiting the search for covered pixels to the vertical range between the polygon's minimum and maximum y-coordinates.

Once the rasterized pixel set R(P) has been determined, the error of a candidate polygon can be measured by comparing the polygon's color to the target image over only those pixels. If cP is the color of the polygon and I(x, y) is the target image color at pixel (x, y), then the sum-of-squared-errors objective can be written as:

SSE(P) = Σ(x,y)∈R(P) || cP - I(x,y) ||2

While we had started with a pure SSE objective function, the algorithm quickly “figured out” that the best way to minimize total SSE was to produce the smallest possible shape. This produced slivers and specks of color, and did not resemble the Mona Lisa. We tried the average SSE next, dividing the total SSE by the number of pixels. While this was effective, it involved costly division every cycle. While this worked fine in C++, it was not well suited for our FPGA implementation. As such, we removed the division and normalized the results by a multiplication of 2^14. This value was found through trial and error, and restricted to a power of 2 for potential further acceleration on the FPGA. We increased this value until we felt that our objective function was appropriately prioritizing the size of the shapes through the duration of the program. We also wanted to have an algorithm that changed as the program progressed - starting with larger shapes (the background, the primary contours, etc) and moving towards the details. The size weight parameter above allowed us to accomplish this, changing the relative weight of num_pixels as seen in equation below.

Score = SSEpolygon - 214wweightNpixel
float r = GET_R_565to332_255(pixel_one) - GET_R_565to332_255(pixel_two); float g = GET_G_565to332_255(pixel_one) - GET_G_565to332_255(pixel_two); float b = GET_B_565to332_255(pixel_one) - GET_B_565to332_255(pixel_two); error += (r * r) + (g * g) + (b * b)

The process of determining which parameters to change over the course of program progression, as well as figuring out how much to change them by, took a significant portion of our design timeline. As previously stated, the high level idea was to force the program to figure out the background and primary contours before moving to finer features.

As seen above, parameters were not transformed linearly, as we found that the program needed to spend relatively more time in the detailed region of parameters. size_weight is the most important parameter, as it controls the extent to which the objective function rewards large shapes. By tuning this parameter, we controlled the progression from background shapes to detail shapes. Furthermore, we found that this parameter helped us perfect our alpha blending. In alpha blending, the new color is produced as a function of the previous color as alpha * new_color + (1 - alpha) * old_color. To avoid nonsensical blending in the early phase of the program, we first fill the canvas with the average color of the painting. We then start with completely opaque shapes such that when we want to layer in semi-transparent, detailed shapes, they are mixing with reasonable colors.

Although the bounding box is not a changing parameter, it was originally designed this way. One of our greatest breakthroughs was realizing that we had to spawn shapes with a small, constant bounding box and allow the algorithm, with a given size_weight, to “grow” the shape into the feature or contour it was near. Furthermore, there is no need to shrink the bounding box over time, as size_weight handles this goal perfectly.

mutate_delta is the maximum displacement (positive or negative) that can be applied to a given vertex mutation. Naturally, we want our program to be able to make larger mutations to the larger shapes, and we want to avoid shapes shifting away from the high-difficulty, fine-feature regions.

Hardware/Software Tradeoffs

A major design choice during the project included dividing computation between the ARM and the FPGA. The software/ARM version of the algorithm was easier to write, test, and debug. Importantly, ARM does not require the lengthy compile times necessary to program Verilog code onto the FPGA, giving us ample opportunity to quickly test new objective functions and tune parameters. Thus, the first half of the project consisted primarily of software development in order to select the optimal algorithmic strategies and parameters.

However, one major downside of using the ARM processor was its long runtime. Specifically, the hill-climbing algorithm had to evaluate every candidate mutation by checking the pixels covered by the polygon and comparing them against the target image. Because the scoring step was required for every mutation, it quickly became one of the main computational bottlenecks in our program. For reference, on the Mona Lisa, the ARM version of the algorithm executed in ~326 seconds, using 100 hill-climbing iterations for 1000 total polygons. To address this speed bottleneck, we exported the polygon scoring step to the FPGA, implementing the algorithm’s key details in Verilog. The Verilog used a state machine to compute rasterization and accumulate the SSE score for each polygon, while running eight parallel iterators to process multiple pixels in each row simultaneously and further improve speed-up. On the Mona Lisa, the hardware-version of the algorithm executed in ~18 seconds, using 100 hill-climbing iterations for 1000 total polygons. For comparison, the hardware scoring-algorithm resulted in an 18.1x speedup and a 94.5% runtime reduction over the ARM version of the algorithm. While the hardware implementation greatly reduced the algorithm’s runtime, it was less flexible than the ARM-based version, offering less opportunity for rapid experimentation and iterative design changes. Due to the added complexity of implementing the polygon scoring in Verilog, we restricted the accelerated scoring algorithm to three-vertex polygons. Consequently, more complex polygons still had to be scored in software on the ARM. Our program dynamically directed computation to the verilog vs. C logic depending on if it matched the logic expected by the hardware (eg: 3 vertices).

This hardware-software split offered us two distinct strengths. The ARM processor provided flexibility for handling complex tasks that would not have been feasible to implement on the FPGA given our resource and time constraints. In contrast, the FPGA provided major speed-up for the repetitive pixel scoring operation that dominated the time complexity of the algorithm’s runtime. The final design therefore incorporated strong hardware acceleration while preserving the benefits of the ARM processor’s flexibility.

Program/Hardware Design

The final system uses C on the ARM as the high-level coordinator and Verilog on the FPGA as the scoring accelerator.

Overall Program Execution

As discussed in the High Level Design section, overall program execution can be summarized in a few steps:

  1. Initialize memory with the reference image.
  2. Run hill climbing: generate an initial baseline polygon, score it, generate and score a sample polygon, select the better score, mutate the selected polygon, and repeat for a chosen number of iterations.
  3. Repeat the hill-climbing process for the chosen number of polygons and draw each accepted polygon to the VGA display.

Initializing the Reference Image

The first step of image preparation involved a Python program which converted a JPEG/JPG into a bitmap, saved in the form of a text file, where each pixel was represented in the RGB, 5:6:5 format to align with the 16-bit color representation used by the VGA. Because the target image varied in size, preprocessing steps allowed the original image dimensions to be adjusted before the image was used by the C program, ensuring clean mapping onto the display region used by the algorithm.

After this conversion, the C program reads the bitmap text file into a global image array, maintaining the 5:6:5 RGB representation which had been established during the image conversion process. We also made sure to rescale each target image, preserving proportionality, to fit within the confines of the usable parts of the VGA screen. For context, our VGA driver required substantial memory, restricting the size of our display to that which could be stored on the FPGA - 320x480 pixels. For uniformity, the selected display pixels for our images were centered on the screen, so the relevant screen pixels spanned pixels 160-480 in the x-direction and 0-480 in the y-direction.

Once the image was properly rescaled and processed, we streamed it to the FPGA through the lightweight PIO bus. For the hardware-accelerated version of the project, we reduced the 16-bit color representations to 8-bit representations to match the structure of the Verilog and maintain consistency across the ARM and the FPGA.

For the image-preparation workflow, ChatGPT helped generate utility code for reading pixel values from a text file into a C array and for modifying the image array to store transformed pixel data before display. The AI-assisted code was reviewed, tested, and modified to match the project’s RGB 5:6:5 color format, VGA coordinate system, and overall image-processing pipeline

Generating and Scoring Polygons

After the reference image was loaded into memory, the ARM’s focus shifted to repeatedly generating, scoring, and mutating polygons. The polygon-scoring step, the most important component of the hill-climbing algorithm, determined how well a candidate polygon matched the underlying target image being reconstructed. This process involved a few key steps:

  1. Generate polygon by randomly mutating a single vertex at a time
  2. Select the color of the polygon using the target-image pixel near the center of the polygon
  3. Rasterize the polygon with a scanline algorithm and compute its sum-of-squared errors objective score over the pixels covered by the polygon

Because the scoring for the algorithm occurred every polygon mutation, it was crucial that the result was correct and that the entire process was efficient. As stated in the Math Background section, the algorithm used rasterization to determine the pixel set over which it evaluated the SSE objective. To determine exactly which pixels each polygon overlapped, our implementation used a scanline algorithm. The algorithm first identified the polygon’s minimum and maximum y-coordinates and then traversed each horizontal row of pixels within this range. For each row, it computed the intersection points between the scanline and the polygon’s edges. The implementation sorted these intersection points by their x-coordinates and treated pixels between alternating pairs of intersections as belonging to the polygon. This approach produced the set of pixels that the polygon overlapped, which the program then used for both the SSE objective and drawing to the VGA display. Note that the original rasterization algorithm, which checked whether each pixel was contained within the polygon, was written from scratch. However, this approach was limited by poor time complexity, as discussed below. The improved version, however, was implemented with assistance from generative AI tools, specifically ChatGPT, demonstrating how AI can be useful for refining and accelerating code development. We later tested, verified, and modified parts of the code to ensure that it was properly integrated into our project’s workflow.

The scanline algorithm also improved the time complexity over the naive pixel-by-pixel containment test, which we had written in draft versions of the algorithm. Suppose the image has a width W and a height H and that the polygon has n vertices. A naive containment approach would check every pixel and determine whether that pixel belongs to the polygon. This standard “pixel-in-polygon” test must check the polygon’s edges and therefore has a worst-case time complexity:

O(W H n)

This becomes inefficient, as many pixels are already far outside of the polygon. Instead of checking every image pixel, our scanline algorithm restricts the search to a smaller set of vertical coordinates. Suppose the polygon spans r rows. Then, the time complexity can be written as:

O(r n + a)

Where a is the number of pixels actually covered by the polygon. r*n comes from the number of rows the polygon spans multiplied by the number of edges that must be checked for each row. Moreover, a comes from scoring each individual pixel contained by the polygon. In this way, the C-version of the Hill-Climbing algorithm experienced nontrivial speed-up relative to more basic versions of our algorithm. However, the largest runtime improvements occurred only after we implemented the scoring algorithm on the FPGA in Verilog. A visual display of the scanline algorithm is displayed below.

In addition to the scanline implementation, a large component of the program design focused on coordinating the full hill-climbing algorithm in C. The ARM/C side of the program controlled image processing, image scaling, polygon mutations, score comparisons, parameter tuning and scheduling, user-interface handling, and VGA drawing. The C thus served as the primary, high-level coordinator for the project. This was true even after the Verilog had been implemented, with the scoring stage of the algorithm being exported to the FPGA. To fully recreate the target image, the program iterated through a user-specified number of mutations for a user-specified number of polygons. And, a Shape struct in C was used for each shape to keep track of its color and vertices, the information required for the algorithm to optimize shape creation. Importantly, the color for each polygon was matched to the color of its center pixel in the target image, giving each candidate shape a color that was related to the image region it tried to approximate.

ARM and FPGA Coordination

Figure 5 illustrates our chosen FPGA:ARM division. The FPGA is responsible only for computing the objective function for a given polygon, sent by the ARM. The ARM sends the x and y coordinates (3 x,y pairs for a triangle), the color of the polygon, and the size weight. These inputs allow the the FPGA to calculate the objective function (SSE - scaled_size_weight * num_pixels) for said polygon and return this value to the ARM. For synchronization, in_valid signals the FPGA to begin computation, out_valid is used to tell the ARM that the new score is ready, and out_ack tells the FPGA that the ARM has received its new score.

The SSE calculations happen num_iterations (defaults to 100) times for each polygon rendered, and the SSE math must occur for every pixel within the given polygon. As such, this step was the natural hardware acceleration we sought on the FPGA. Furthermore, we were able to take advantage of parallelization to send multiple iterators on the SSE computation, resulting in further acceleration. Our parallelization architecture (each iterator working on its own subset of pixels, with its own slice of the target image) required no changes to the ARM:FPGA interface, and could therefore be abstracted away to the verilog portion of the design. This simplified our integration and debugging immensely.

Figure 6 presents our configured Avalon bus. It’s worth noting that our most time-intensive bug was due to an incorrect bit width in the third y coordinate. We could not figure out why certain shapes were being scored poorly in the verilog logic, and spent all our time looking for a fault in the math or state machine. This was a good lesson in not assuming the source of your bug without verification.

Hardware Design

The hardware contains the reference image in an M10K block. It is responsible for calculating the final score given the coordinates and color of a polygon, as well as driving the VGA display. We implemented two versions of the accelerator to score the generated polygon: an unoptimized and an optimized version. We will discuss both designs in this section. We used AI to help us get an initial boilerplate based off of the C code, which we manually modified and debugged.

VGA Driver

We use the 16 bit color VGA display from the SDRAM. This part of the FPGA is created in isolation from the rest of the logic. It does not interact with the M10K block, nor does it interface with the polygon scoring module. It only interfaces with HPS. We took the template code from the ECE 5760 webpage. From a high level, the C code sends the pixels it wants to draw, which is stored in the SDRAM on the FPGA. The VGA DMA driver reads directly from the SDRAM, driving the VGA display

Reference image initialization

We use an M10K of depth 320 x 480, where each entry is 8 bits. The reason we’re using 8 bit colors on the FPGA but 16 bit colors on the C is due to the limited available memory. The accelerator will work with 8 bit colors to conserve memory, whilst the C-program as well as the VGA display will use 16 bit colors. The C-program sends a write enable signal, the x and y coordinates of each pixel (which are transformed into M10K write addresses). It also converts the 16 bit color to 8 bits before sending it to the FPGA. Notably, the 16 bit color produces a much more visually appealing final product, especially in relation to the alpha blending at lower transparencies.

Unoptimized Polygon Scoring Accelerator

To calculate the score for each polygon, the C code must provide the FPGA with the x and y coordinates of each vertex, the 8 bit color, and a weight used to get the final polygon score. Similar to C, the verilog state machine iterates through every pixel inside the polygon. For each polygon pixel, it fetches the corresponding pixel from the reference image and accumulates the SSE. Beside the 8 bit vs 16 bit color difference, the verilog implementation also had other algorithmic differences from C due to hardware limitations.

Where the verilog deviates from C is how we calculate which pixel is inside the polygon. Where both programs use scan-line algorithms, the C finds the bounds of each row using the slope of each edge of the polygon. In Verilog, on the other hand, since we avoided using division, we instead used the Bresenham Algorithm, where we kept track of the dy, dx and an error value in place of the slope. We could’ve used Altera’s lpm_divider, but we decided to keep our design generic, so it is very easily replicable by other people.

Another place where the verilog deviated from C is when we scanned each row for hit, we only looked for at most two hits per row. The implication is that the verilog could only use convex shapes. The left diagram in Figure 8 shows a general polygon, which can have more than two hits per row. The one on the right shows a triangle (or any convex polygon), which has maximum two hits per row. To keep things simple, we made sure that the C code only sends triangles to the FPGA, which is always guaranteed convex. We made this design decision to keep the logic more compact, but at the cost of losing hardware flexibility.

In Figure 9 and Table 1, we elaborate on a diagram of the state machine that calculates the SSE per pixel, and finds the next pixel using the Bresenham Algorithm. The accelerator uses a ready-valid handshake protocol. The HPS asserts in_val when polygon data is ready, and the FPGA responds with in_rdy when it can accept new work. Upon completion, the FPGA asserts out_val, and waits for the HPS to acknowledge with out_ack before accepting new polygons.

Floating-Point Handling

All of the SSE calculations are done in integer format. The final scoring, however, is done in floating point. In an earlier section, we discussed the objective function:

Score = SSEpolygon - 214 wsize Npixels

We keep track of Npixels through an integer accumulator, so we need to convert it as well as SSEpolygon into floating point numbers. The input “weight” was already in 32 bit floating point format. We instantiated two floating point multiplication blocks for 214wsizeNpixels , an fp addition for the final score calculation. The fp adder has 2 cycles delay, which we also took into account in our state machine. The adder starts calculating on update edges, so the result would be done by calc score, where we latch the result to the output.

Optimized Polygon Scoring Accelerator

To further increase the acceleration benefits of the FPGA, we implemented multiple pixel iterators in Verilog so that the hardware could process several pixels in parallel during the scoring operation. Instead of evaluating one covered pixel at a time, the accelerator used multiple iterator partitions, allowing it to compute several sum-of-squared error values simultaneously. To allow for these parallel reads, the top level Verilog module split the target image across multiple separate M10K memory banks. Each pixel was assigned to a bank based upon its flattened linear image address modulo the number of iterators used by the accelerator, while its address within that bank was computed by dividing the linear address by the number of iterators. During the scoring operation, each iterator requested a VGA coordinate, and the top level module converted that coordinate into the same flattened address used to determine the correct M10K and bank address in the first place. This scheme thus allowed for multiple iterators to process different pixels in the same cycle, enabling the FPGA to run the scanline scoring algorithm in parallel.

Because of the way the memory was designed, it was most practical to use a quantity of iterators chosen as a power of 2 (e.g., 1, 4, 2, 8). We could not, however, use 16 or more iterators because of FPGA timing constraints. When attempting a run with 16 iterators, the resulting timing report indicated that all logical operations could not reliably meet the timing requirements of the 50MHz clock cycle, leading to an additional unforeseen computational bottleneck in our algorithm’s workflow. To address this issue in future iterations of the design, the FPGA clock could be slowed to a frequency below 50MHz to accommodate 16 iterators, trading a faster clock rate for more parallel computational bandwidth. This modification, while slowing down the cycle time, would allow for double the parallelism, potentially leading to additional hardware speedup.

Let each pixel in the 320 x 480 target image be indexed by its image coordinate (x,y). The corresponding flattened address is:

A = yW + x

where W=320 is the image width. To split the image across N M10K memory banks, where N is the number of pixel iterators, the bank index is computed as

b = A mod N

and the address within that bank is computed as:

ab = ⌊ A / N ⌋

For comparison, this speed-up scheme reduced the execution time for the Mona Lisa from 23.392 seconds to 18.293 seconds, yielding a 21.7% decrease in timing. Limitations

Our design is very memory bound. Because we need to store the entire image in M10K on chip, we’re limited by the number of copies of the image we can store as well as other components that use memory. One implication of that is we can’t use M10Ks as a VGA buffer, which would be faster than our current implementation, which uses SDRAMS as the buffer. Another constraint is we can’t operate on multiple polygons at the same time, which limits how much we can speed up the hill climbing function. Nonetheless, our workaround, which partitioned one polygon to multiple pixel iterators, was decently efficient.

User Interface

We chose to write a simple but robust user interface through the serial terminal wherein the user enters a key to select which command they wish to make, then enter the value for that command. If the program does not recommend the command, it will inform the user. If the program detects a value outside of the command’s expected range, it will reject that value and inform the user.

From top to bottom of the Figure 13 commands, num_polygons lets the user control how many shapes they want to recreate their chosen artwork. A low number of shapes will be more abstract but run faster. A high number of shapes will approach total realism but be extremely slow. num_vertices is exactly what you’d expect, wherein the user can select a line (2 vertices), a triangle (3 vertices), or higher-vertice shapes (4-10). As the verilog was constrained to only handle triangles, the C program routes the SSE calculations for any other num_vertices away from the verilog. num_iterations presents a similar tradeoff to the num_shapes in that an increase in num_iterations may improve the image quality but will certainly delay the program. Through this user interface, we found that there are diminishing returns in num_iterations higher than 100. Furthermore, you will get very small shapes for a low num_iterations as our algorithm spawns shapes at 10x10 or less, then grows them with each iteration. The last numerical parameter is end_alpha. Nominally, the program starts with fully opaque polygons (alpha = 1.0) and transitions to mostly transparent polygons (alpha = 0.3) over the course of the program. The user may control the end_alpha value to produce more blending and a more transparent final product. This weights the additional transparency towards the fine features (smaller polygons) which does produce a very nicely-blended image.

The mode is a command of its own which lets the user modify the art style as per the below:

  • NORMAL
  • RED_SHIFT, BLUE_SHIFT, GREEN_SHIFT
    • Modifies the red, green, and blue components before graphing to accentuate the chosen color.
    • Example: RED_SHIFT becomes (red, green / 4, blue / 4).
  • HALLUCINATE
    • This was born out of a typo in which we accidentally bitwise blended the red, green, and blue values in their entirety instead of blending each component separately.
    • The result was an awesome psychedelic artwork that still resembled the Mona Lisa.
    • We then programmed this bug to become an optional feature.
  • PAINT
    • This was also inspired by a typo, where I accidentally constrained the pixel mutations to strictly add to x and y.
    • This only allowed polygons to mutate toward the bottom-right corner, creating a paint-stroke effect.
    • We also turned this bug into an optional feature.

Only the NORMAL mode can run within our relatively strict verilog logic. The other modes all involve significant changes to the optimization function logic. With more time, we could send the modes to the FPGA and modify its logic accordingly. This would reduce the slow-ARM runtimes for the different modes.

Our program generates random polygons, but for the purpose of this comparison table, we initialized the seed to a constant “42”. The three versions produced three exact same Mona Lisa’s as shown in Table 2, our final, optimized design reduced rendering time by almost 95% (18 x speed up).

Conclusions

This is the first time that an image evolution algorithm has been accelerated by hardware. The speed up was quite considerable without compromising the outcome of the design. While it built on prior designs as previously described, the algorithm was a significant departure from anything built previously. We did not reuse code or anyone else’s design, nor did we use any of Altera’s IPs. Overall, we’re very happy with how our design turned out.

As a whole, we integrated generative AI (primarily ChatGPT and Gemini) into our workflow but did not allow it to take over the design process nor write all of our code. We wrote certain functions, cited in the code and mentioned in this report, with AI where the result could be proven to be correct. We also used AI in our debugging process, feeding both the faulty output and select portions of our code to AI and using our judgement to see which of its ideas may be worth trying. Finally, we allowed AI to help format our website and generate some of the HTML. It did not in any way write our content or create our figures.

There are a lot of opportunities for further optimization in our final design, judging by how little resources we’ve used in our final design.

One idea is to add even more pixel iterators. Currently we’re at 8 iterators. Adding more iterators caused a setup time issue when we tried it, but it’s possible to slow down the clock with a PPL. However, increasing the number of iterators from 1 to 8 only incurred a ~5 second speed up. Our suspicion is that the speed of HPS communication is our main bottleneck. If we could limit the number of transactions by offloading the entire hill climbing function would incur a much faster speed up. The hill climbing function mutates the polygon based on the calculated SSE. We could emulate the random mutations using a linear feedback shift register (LFSR), and directly drive the VGA display in verilog instead of C.
